title: Architect the Solution Architecture (Method)
overview: The method develops requirements, logical architecture and physical architecture through repeated outline, detail and review work. Each activity has ten tasks with named roles and work products. The IROne reservation example shows how requirements lead to components, deployment choices and documented decisions; revisit earlier assumptions when validation exposes a problem.
big_ideas: The method answers four questions: **When** (phases and iterations), **Who** (roles), **What** (work products) and **How** (activities made of tasks).
Three activities: Define Requirements, Logical Architecture and Physical Architecture. Logical and physical work each include outline, detail and review; iterate when new evidence changes the design.
Requirements work produces: stakeholder requests, glossary, system context, functional and non-functional requirements, prioritised requirements, and a reviewed Solution Architecture Document.
Architecturally significant requirements: critical functionality (80/20), critical quality, critical constraint, or technical/architectural risk.
Logical architecture is technology-neutral: architecture overview, functional model (boundary, control, entity components) and deployment model (locations, nodes).

Physical architecture realises the logical one with real technology (e.g. Java EE): logical elements map one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-one onto physical elements, and nodes are sized to the non-functional requirements.
Every significant choice is recorded as an architecture decision (issue, decision, assumptions, alternatives, justification), and risk is reduced by verification, validation and a proof-of-concept.
The architect owns the Solution Architecture Document and must keep artefacts baselined and reviewed with stakeholders.

sections.title: Fundamentals of the method
sections.summary: A method defines when, who, what and how; the architecture work sits inside a Unified Process style lifecycle and flows from requirements to logical to physical architecture.

items: **Who** → roles: responsibilities of a person or team
**What** → work products: information produced or used
**How** → activities, each a group of tasks; a **task** is a unit of work with a meaningful result

notes.h: Architecting is iterative, not a one-off
notes.foot: **Outline** work happens in the **architecture discipline**; **detailing** leans into **development**.

items: **Eeles and Cripps**, The Process of Software Architecting
Focuses on **how to architect** → requirements, logical and physical architecture, role of the architect

terms.def: Information or entity produced and/or used by tasks (e.g. system context, functional model).
A grouping of tasks; here Define Requirements, Logical Architecture and Physical Architecture.
Popular iterative framework with Inception, Elaboration, Construction and Transition phases.

check.q: A team's process document lists tasks such as 'design the database' and 'write tests', but not who does them, what each produces or when they happen. What is missing, and why does it matter?

a.lead: It has the **'how'** (activities and tasks) but not the rest of a method:
items: **'What'**: **work products** → without them nobody can tell when a task is **done** or what the next task takes as **input**
a.foot: Adding them turns a **to-do list** into a **method** that can be planned and reviewed.

check.q: A project manager plans to start architecture work in Construction, 'once there is some code to look at'. Critique the plan.

items: **Unified Process**: architecture effort **peaks in Elaboration** → the key **structural decisions and risks** must be settled before heavy construction
**Starting late** → building on **unvalidated assumptions** and paying for **rework**
**Construction**: architecture does continue, as **detailing and refinement**, but it should not start there

check.q: While detailing the physical architecture, the team learns that the payment provider accepts only batch files. Does the method require starting again from requirements?

items: **Record the new constraint** in the requirements
**Revisit the affected logical elements** (the payment boundary and its control flow)
**Update the physical design** and **record the decision**
a.foot: Only the parts the constraint touches need to change.

sections.title: Requirements I: stakeholders, vocabulary and system context
sections.summary: The first tasks of Define Requirements build the shared understanding: who cares, what the words mean, and what is inside and outside the system.

notes.foot: Every task is described by **roles, inputs, outputs** and **architect-specific tips**.

items: Architect makes sure **technical stakeholders are included** → system administrator, owners of external systems
Captures **qualities and constraints**, not just features
**Helps prioritise** → explains the **cost and time-to-market impact** of one request over another
**Define terms once and consistently**, especially **technical** ones
**IROne** → Reservation, Amenity, Reservation Agent, Amenity Operator
**Identify actors** → include **external systems** such as the **payment gateway**
**Identify actor locations** → if an actor is found at **several locations**, introduce a **new actor per location**
**Identify data flows** between actors (including external systems) and the system
**Central Office** → holds owner, administrator, agents and the payment system

terms.def: A need, quality or constraint raised by anyone with an interest in the system.
Agreed definitions of the domain and technical terms used in the project.
The system as a black box with its actors, their locations and the data flows to and from it.

check.q: Stakeholder workshops for a hospital booking system included doctors, patients and the operations director only. What is missing, and what is likely to go wrong?

items: **Missing: technical stakeholders** → **system administrators** and the **owners of external systems** such as the patient-record and payment systems
**Risk**: business stakeholders rarely state **availability, operability and integration constraints** → they surface late and force **rework**
**Architect's job**: make sure **qualities and constraints** are collected, not just features

check.q: In a resort system, reservation agents work both at the central office and at each hotel's front desk, with different network access. How do you show them in the system context, and why?

a.lead: Introduce a **separate actor for each location**, such as **Central Office Reservation Agent** and **Hotel Reservation Agent**. Each can then be:
a.foot: Cost: a slightly larger **context diagram**, in exchange for not hiding **location-specific requirements**.

check.q: Sales uses 'booking' to mean a confirmed, paid reservation, while operations uses it for any held slot. Why does the architect care?

items: **Effect**: **capacity counts**, **reports** and **integration messages** would disagree about what a booking is
**Fix**: capture a **common vocabulary** early and define each term **once**
a.foot: Fixing it **after the data model is built** is far more expensive.

sections.title: Requirements II: outlining functional and non-functional requirements
sections.summary: Outline what the system does for each actor and which qualities it must meet, stating clearly what is out of scope.

items: **IROne** → Search Slot, Reserve Slot, Administer Reservations, View Sales Report (each with its **primary actors**)

notes.foot: These are **outlines**: detail the **workload, measurement period and acceptance conditions** before sizing or testing.

terms.def: A capability the system must provide to an actor (e.g. Reserve Slot).
A quality or constraint such as availability, performance, scalability or integration.

check.q: An NFR reads: 'Search shall respond in under 3 seconds.' What would you add before using it for sizing or testing?

items: **Measurement boundary**: server only or **end to end**
**Average or percentile**: e.g. 3 s for 90% of requests
a.foot: Without them, two teams can test the same system and both claim **compliance** with different results.

check.q: Is 'supports 1000 concurrent users' enough to size the servers?
check.a: No. Specify what users do, their request mix and think time, and the required response times. A concurrent-user count alone does not determine the request rate or the work each request needs.

check.q: The functional outline for a reservation system lists only customer use cases. Later, operations asks how to cancel a stuck reservation. What went wrong?

items: **Per actor**: functional requirements should be outlined per actor in the **system context**, including **technical users** such as administrators and operators
**Missing 'Administer Reservations'** → the function and its **data access** are added late → **rework**
**Scope**: the outline should also confirm explicitly what is **out of scope**

check.q: Search must be 99.9% available, and every other function 99%. What does this split let the architect do?

items: **Search (99.9%)**: give it extra **redundancy** and **isolate** it from the less critical functions
**Instead of** paying for 99.9% across the whole system
a.foot: Cost: a more complex **deployment** with **separately scaled** parts → worth it only if search can actually **run independently** of the 99% components.

sections.title: Requirements III: prioritise, detail, document and review
sections.summary: Pick the architecturally significant requirements, detail them as use cases and NFR scenarios, record them in the Solution Architecture Document, then review with stakeholders.

items: Relate to **critical functionality** without which there is **no viable system** (use the **80/20 rule**)
Relate to a **critical quality** such as **performance**
Relate to a **critical constraint** such as **integration with a specific external system**
Carry a particular **technical or architectural risk**
notes.foot: The architect **articulates the trade-offs** during prioritisation.

notes.h: Detail functional requirements as use cases
notes.lead: Focus on the **significant** ones. Each use case has:

items.t: **Alternative flows**, each returning to a defined step, e.g.:

items: Architect also helps define **data items** and **system-wide functions** such as **online help**

notes.lead: **Owned by the architect**; based on **ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010** (formerly **IEEE 1471**). Structure:

items: **Changes** flow through a **change request** and **request log**
Treat the system as a **black box** → **no tiers or technology**
Include **inputs, outputs** and **information reads and writes**

terms.def: A requirement that shapes the architecture: critical function, quality or constraint, or one that carries technical risk.
Stimulus, source, artifact, environment, response and response measure describing a quality testably.
The linkage from requirements to the solution elements that satisfy them.
A reviewed, agreed version of an artefact that later changes must go through change control.

check.q: For a ticketing system, which of these are architecturally significant, and why: (a) the colour of the 'print receipt' button; (b) handling 30,000 buyers in the first 5 minutes of a sale; (c) integration with a national ID service's fixed API; (d) a streaming library nobody on the team has used?

items: **(a) Not significant**: a **detail** with no architectural impact
a.foot: Significant requirements **shape the structure** and are worth **detailing first**, because they are **costly to change later**.

check.q: Rewrite 'the system shall be available' as a six-part availability scenario for a payment-gateway outage.

items: **Response**: detect the failure, hold orders and tell customers that payment is pending
**Response measure**: detection within 30 s, no confirmed order lost, and checkout degraded for no more than 10 minutes
a.foot: Each part now gives the architect something to **design and test** against.

check.q: Late in the project, a stakeholder asks to drop the 'check hotel availability' requirement. How does the Solution Architecture Document help?

items: **Traceability section**: links the requirement to the **components, interfaces and decisions** that satisfy it → see what would be removed or simplified and **estimate the impact**
**Process**: handle the change through a **change request** and the **review process**, and **record the outcome**

steps.label: 1-3 Understand
steps.detail: Collect stakeholder requests, capture common vocabulary, define the system context (actors, locations, data flows).

steps.label: 4-5 Outline
steps.detail: Outline what the system does for each actor and the qualities it must meet.

steps.label: 6 Prioritize
steps.detail: Pick architecturally significant requirements and articulate the trade-offs between them.

steps.label: 7-8 Detail
steps.detail: Detail the significant requirements: use cases with alternative flows, and NFR scenarios with a response measure.

steps.label: 9 Update SAD
steps.detail: Record requirements and decisions in the Solution Architecture Document.

steps.label: 10 Review
steps.detail: Baseline artefacts and answer technical questions; record in a review record.

sections.title: Logical architecture: the ten tasks and surveying assets
sections.summary: The logical architecture activity outlines then details functional and deployment elements; it starts by surveying reusable assets and recording decisions.

items: **Outline** gives the **structure**; **detail** adds **signatures, contracts and assignments**
**Roles** → Solution, Software, Data and Infrastructure Architect

notes.foot: The **same ten-task list repeats** for the **physical** activity.

items: Look for **reusable assets** → **reference patterns** and **reference architectures**
If a **reference architecture or packaged solution** is used → architect may spend **less effort on logical** and **more on physical**

notes.lead: Decisions and constraints are **justification** referenced in later phases. Template:

items: **Why** → only about **30 rules** (at most **40**) are expected
**Alternative: buy a commercial engine** → overkill, not cost effective
**Alternative: embed rules in code** → violates **separation of concerns** and **decoupling**, harder to maintain

terms.def: Recorded issue, decision, assumptions, alternatives and justification for a significant architectural choice.
A reusable, proven template architecture for a class of systems.
Outline defines elements and structure; detail adds interfaces, signatures, contracts and assignments.

check.q: IROne built a custom rules engine on the assumption of about 30 to 40 rules. A year later, marketing wants 400 rules editable by business users. What does the decision record tell you to do?

a.lead: The recorded **assumption** no longer holds → the decision must be **reviewed**.
items: **Recorded alternatives** may now be justified, such as buying a **commercial rules engine** that was overkill at 30 rules
**Reassess** against the new needs rather than **switching automatically**
a.foot: This is why decisions record **assumptions and alternatives** as well as the choice.

check.q: A client buys a packaged reservation product that covers 70% of the required functions. How does this change where architecture effort goes?

items: **Less effort on logical structure**: the package supplies much of it
**More effort on physical architecture**: fitting and **configuring the package**, and **integrating** the remaining 30%
**Risk shifts**: the package's **constraints** now limit the design → record them as **decisions**

check.q: A decision log entry reads only 'Decision: use a message queue for hotel integration.' What is wrong with it?

a.lead: It lacks the **issue, assumptions, alternatives and justification**. Later teams cannot tell:
items: **What change** (in **volume or latency** needs, for instance) should **trigger a review**
a.foot: Record the full template: **Issue, Decision, Assumptions, Alternatives, Justification**.

visuals.title: Logical architecture: outline vs detail
rows: Interface, operation, signature, mapping to data, pre/post-conditions

sections.title: Logical architecture: overview and functional elements
sections.summary: Draw an overview of layers and zones from the system context, then identify boundary, control and entity components per use case.

items: **Starts from the system context** and **adds subsystems**
Cover the **key logical structure** → layers, locations and their relationships

sub: **Internal Zone 1** → web, application, rules and integration tiers
**Internal Zone 2** → hotel, show, park and payment systems

notes.h: Outline functional elements: three component types
items: **Boundary** → interface to a **primary actor**, or to an **external system** to send or get data
**Control** → **coordination logic**; **one controller per use case**, split into **sub-controllers** only if too complex

sub: **hotel, show, park and payment system interfaces** (boundary)

items: **Reuse and review** components identified for earlier use cases

terms.def: Handles interaction between the system and its environment (actor UI or external system interface).
Coordinates the logic of a use case; typically one controller per use case.
Encapsulates and manages the information held by the system.

check.q: For a 'Cancel Booking' use case: the customer's web page, the logic that coordinates the cancellation and refund rules, the link to the payment gateway, and the Booking record. Classify each and say how many controllers you would start with.

a.foot: Start with **one controller for the use case**; split it into **sub-controllers** only if it becomes too complex.

check.q: A design has one 'ReservationManager' component that renders screens, applies rules, calls the hotel system and stores the data. What is wrong, in robustness-analysis terms?

items: **Problem**: it mixes **boundary, control and entity** responsibilities → a change to a screen, a rule or the hotel interface affects one large component

sub: **Boundaries**: a reservation UI and a hotel-system interface

a.foot: Cost: more components and interfaces → in return **changes stay local**.

check.q: The architecture overview leaves out the payment system that appears in the system context. How should this be caught?

items: **Trace** every **actor, external system and data flow** from the **system context** into the **overview**
The **payment system** needs a **boundary** or **integration-layer** element
a.foot: Starting the overview from the context makes such omissions visible, but only if someone **checks it item by item**.

center.label: Reserve Slot Control
center.detail: The controller for the Reserve Slot use case; coordinates the UI, the rules check, the amenity and payment systems and the stored reservation.

items.label: Reservation UI
items.detail: Interface to the customer or reservation agent.

items.label: Reservation Rules Checker
items.detail: Verifies the slot against business rules.

items.label: Amenity interfaces
items.detail: Interfaces to the external amenity systems to make the booking.

items.label: Payment System Interface
items.detail: Interface to the payment gateway to take payment.

sections.title: Logical architecture: deployment, verify, validate, review
sections.summary: Place logical components on logical nodes and locations, then verify and validate the architecture and review it with stakeholders.

items: At this stage nodes are **purely logical containers**
**Central Office** → web, application, rules, integration and database servers

notes.lead: **Verification** is a **review of the outlined architecture**:

items: Creates an **architectural proof-of-concept** to **reduce risk** (from a **conceptual sketch** to a **working prototype**)
**Update the Solution Architecture Document** (architect is responsible)

terms.def: A sketch or prototype that tests key architectural assumptions to reduce risk.
A concern such as security or logging that spans many components and must be handled consistently.
Contract on an operation: what must hold before it is called and what it guarantees afterwards.

check.q: The team doubts whether the rules engine can evaluate 40 rules within the 3-second search target. Is a verification meeting enough?

items: **Verification** reviews the outlined architecture for **consistency** and **cross-cutting concerns** → it cannot measure performance

sub: **Measure** it against the 3 s target with a **realistic load**

check.q: A logical deployment model labels the application node '2 x 16-core, 64 GB'. A reviewer objects. Why?

items: **Logical nodes** only say which **kinds of node** exist, in which **locations**, and what runs on them
a.foot: Fixing hardware before the **technology is chosen** and the **NFRs are sized** commits the design early and **without evidence**.

check.q: Two teams will build components that call each other, and so far they have agreed only on component names. What must the detailed functional model add before they code?

a.foot: Without these, each team will assume different behaviour and the **mismatch appears at integration**.

sections.title: Physical architecture: assets, overview and mapping to technology
sections.summary: The physical activity repeats the ten tasks but chooses concrete technology, mapping each logical element onto physical ones.

items: **IROne constraint** → run in a **Java EE server**
**Justification** → existing **skills** in developing and deploying on WebSphere
**One to one** → a **single physical element** satisfies the **full specification**
**One to many** → one logical element realised by **several physical elements**, e.g. for **availability**
**Many to one** → several logical elements realised by **one physical element**, e.g. a **packaged application**

notes.foot: This is **one technology choice**, not a universal mapping rule.

terms.def: Java EE server-side component used to implement controller logic.
Java Message Service: messaging used to integrate with external systems.
Java Persistence API: maps entity components to a relational database.

check.q: Logical 'Reservation Control' must meet 99.9% availability. Logical 'Reporting', 'Billing' and 'CRM' are all covered by one packaged product. Which logical-to-physical mapping applies to each, and what does each cost?

sub: Several **physical instances**, so one failure does not stop the service
One physical element realises several logical ones (Reporting, Billing, CRM)
**Cost**: ties them to that product's **release cycle and limits**

check.q: A team maps every logical component, including the hotel-system interfaces, to synchronous REST controllers. The hotel systems are reachable only through message queues. Critique the mapping.

items: **Rule**: each logical element must be mapped to technology that meets its **specification and constraints**
**System-facing boundary** to queue-only hotel systems → **messaging** (IROne used **JMS**)
a.foot: **Record the mapping choice per element** as a decision, rather than applying one technology everywhere.

check.q: IROne chose an application server product because the team already had skills in it. A new CTO says to always choose the cheapest licence. How do you respond?

items: **Existing skills** reduce **delivery and operating risk**, which is part of the solution's **viability**
**Cheapest licence** may not be the **cheapest solution** once **training, mistakes and slower delivery** are counted
a.foot: If the team's **skills change** or **licence cost** becomes dominant, **revisit the decision**.

sections.title: Physical architecture: deployment, sizing and integration
sections.summary: Define physical nodes sized to the NFRs, deploy components to them, specify integration endpoints, and summarise the deliverables.

items: For each **logical location** → define **how many physical instances**
For each **logical node** → define the **physical node(s)**
**Web server** → IBM pSeries, 2 x 2.0 GHz, 16 GB, AIX, Apache
**Application server** → 4 x 2.0 GHz, 32 GB, WebSphere, DB2, Java programs for rules
**Integration server** → 2 x 2.0 GHz, 16 GB, IBM MQ Series
Show **packages (WAR, JAR)** deployed to nodes and **manifesting the classes**

items.t: Same logical design can be **redeployed in a microservice style**, e.g.:
sub: on **Amazon EC2** via **ECS**, with **Spring Boot** in **Docker** images

items: **To show, hotel and park systems** → **JMS** with **XML**
notes.foot: Two links having **different formats alone** does not explain the **exact mapping** needed.

items: **Logical architecture** → overview, functional model, deployment model
**Physical architecture** → overview, functional model, deployment model
notes.foot: **Exercise 2** applies the physical steps to the **Student Health System**.

terms.def: A connection between two systems defined by source, destination, protocol, format and transformation.
Choosing CPU, memory and instances for a node to meet NFRs.

check.q: Requirements: 1000 concurrent users and 99.9% search availability. A physical design has one web server and one application server, each sized for 1,200 users. Does it meet the NFRs?

a.lead: **Capacity** may be enough, but **availability is not met**.
items: **Fix**: at least **two nodes per tier**, sized so that the **survivors still handle 1000 users** when one fails
**Confirm** availability and capacity with the **real workload**

check.q: The requirements specify web-service integration, but the physical example uses JMS. What should the architect do?
check.a: Treat it as a traceability issue. Confirm whether an approved decision changed the requirement or an adapter satisfies it; otherwise revise the physical design. The example's technology mapping alone is not evidence of compliance.

check.q: The integration endpoint table shows client to web over HTTPS/HTML, and application to hotel systems over messaging with XML, marked 'transformation: yes'. What work does that flag create?

a.lead: It flags an **adapter** that maps the application's **structures** to the hotel systems' **formats and meanings**, which must be **specified and tested**.
items: The flag says mapping is **needed**; it does not **define** it
Use of **XML or messaging** alone does not prove a transformation is needed

check.q: The same logical design must be redeployed as containerised microservices. What changes and what stays?

items: **Largely stays**: the **logical functional model** (components, interfaces, contracts)

items.t: **Changes**: the **physical deployment** → nodes become **containers** grouped into **services**
sub: Such as a **reservation service** with its **own database**

items: **Redo**: **endpoints**, **sizing** and the **deployment mapping**, **validated against the NFRs**

layers.label: Client PC (Internet)
layers.detail: Customer's machine, in the Internet location.

layers.label: Web Server
layers.detail: Serves the presentation layer (JSPs and servlets in a WAR) over HTTP/HTTPS.

layers.label: Application Server
layers.detail: Hosts control (session EJBs), data access (JPA), rules and persistence; the largest node.

layers.label: Integration Server
layers.detail: Messaging via JMS with XML to the hotel, show, park and payment systems.

exam_angles.q: A clinic chain wants online booking within 6 months: 40 clinics, about 2,000 concurrent users at 8 am, and integration with a patient-record system that only accepts batch files overnight. (a) Pick three architecturally significant requirements and justify each. (b) Write one as a six-part scenario. (c) What decision would you record about the patient-record integration?

sub: **8 am peak of 2,000 concurrent users** → **critical quality**: drives capacity and scaling
**Booking itself** → **critical functionality**: without it there is no viable system

items.t: **(c) Decision record** for the patient-record integration
sub: **Issue**: bookings must reach patient records, but only overnight batch is possible
**Decision**: store bookings in the booking system and export them nightly
**Alternatives**: real-time integration, which is not offered
**Revisit** if same-day record access becomes a requirement

exam_angles.q: A requirements document says: 'The system must be fast, secure and user-friendly and support 1000 users.' It lists only customer use cases. As architect, critique it and say what you would do in Define Requirements.

sub: The user count gives no **request mix** or **think time**
Collect requests from **technical stakeholders** too (administrators, owners of external systems)
Build a **glossary** and a **system context** with **actors per location**
Outline **functional requirements per actor**, including **administration**, and **NFRs with targets and conditions**
**Prioritise** the **architecturally significant** ones and detail them as **use cases** and **six-part scenarios**
Record them in the **SAD** with **traceability**, and **review** with stakeholders

exam_angles.q: For a 'Transfer Ticket' use case (an owner transfers a ticket to a friend, the system checks transfer rules and notifies an external venue system), derive the boundary, control and entity components, then propose a physical mapping that supports high availability.

items: **Boundaries**: the transfer UI (owner) and the venue-system interface (external)
**Control**: **Transfer Ticket control**, which coordinates the rules check, possibly using a **rules component**

sub: **Control → stateless application component**, deployed **one to many** across several instances
**Venue interface → messaging**, so venue outages don't block transfers

a.foot: **Record each choice as a decision** and check it against the **availability target**.

exam_angles.q: Logical model: web, application, rules and integration nodes at the central office. NFRs: 1000 concurrent users with 99.9% availability. A benchmark shows one application node handles 400 users at the response target. Size the physical application tier and explain your mapping.

items: **Survive one node failure**: the survivors must still carry 1000 users → **4 nodes** (3 survivors x 400 = 1,200)
**Mapping**: a **one-to-many** mapping of the logical application node → requires **stateless components** or **shared session state**, and a **load balancer**
**Confirm** the 400-user figure with the **production request mix**, since benchmarks do not scale perfectly

exam_angles.q: A validation proof of concept shows the integration server handles 50 messages/s, but the peak need is 120 messages/s. How does this finding flow through the method, and what options would you weigh?

items: **Validation** documents the finding, its **risk** and **recommendations**, **traced to the NFR** it threatens

sub: **Deploy the integration node one to many**: three instances give about **150 messages/s** if it scales, which **must be measured**
**Batch or queue** messages to **smooth the peak**, if a short delay is acceptable

items: **Record** the chosen option as a **decision** with its **assumptions**, **update the SAD** and **review** it with stakeholders
**Repeat validation** until the risk is acceptable
